data.name: Ashur
data.gender_notes: Ashur is used as a male name in Christian naming traditions.
data.short_meaning: Assyrian god of war and hunting
data.long_meaning: Derived from the Assyrian language, Ashur was the name of the chief god of the Assyrians, a people from ancient Mesopotamia. He was the god of war, the protector of cities, and the god of hunting. In the Bible, Ashur is mentioned several times as a place or as the name of an Assyrian king. The name Ashur carries the meaning “Assyrian god of war and hunting” and is chosen by families in Christian traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Biblical tradition and is also used in English, Greek, Latin. Parents who choose Ashur usually hope their child will grow to embody assyrian god of war and hunting and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: Symbol of strength, protection, and courage
data.etymology: Ashur belongs to the Biblical linguistic tradition and is used in Christian naming. Its recorded meaning is “Assyrian god of war and hunting.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Ashur total 4, giving a life-path number of 4. Number 4 is linked with Rahu and with the qualities of stability, discipline and hard work.

in_hebrew.name: אשור
in_hebrew.meaning: עיר או ארץ באזור המזרח התיכון הקדום
in_hebrew.long_meaning: השם אשור הוא שמו של בן בכורו של שֵׁם בֶּן אַרפַּכְשָׁד, בנו של נוֹח, וכן שם של עיר או ארץ באזור המזרח התיכון הקדום. האֵשורִים היו צאצאיו של אשור, והוא עצמו היה בנו של שֵׁם. האזור נקרא על שמו של האשורִים, שהיו עם חשוב באזור זה בתקופת המקרא.

in_greek.name: Ἀσσουρ
in_greek.meaning: Πόλη ή περιοχή στην αρχαία Ανατολή
in_greek.long_meaning: Ὁ Ἀσσουρ εἶναι ὁ πρωτόγονος υἱὸς τοῦ Σήμ, τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ Νώε, καὶ ὄνομα πόλεως ἢ περιοχῆς στὴν ἀρχαία Μεσοποταμία. Οἱ Ἀσσύριοι, ἦσαν οἱ απόγονοι τοῦ Ἀσσουρ καὶ αὐτός ὁ Ἀσσουρ ἦταν υἱὸς τοῦ Σήμ. Ἡ περιοχή ὀνομάστηκε ἀπὸ τοὺς Ἀσσυρίους, ποὺ ἦσαν σημαντικὸς λαὸς ἐκεῖ.

in_latin.name: Assur
in_latin.meaning: City or region in ancient Mesopotamia
in_latin.long_meaning: Assur is the name of the eldest son of Shem, son of Arphaxad, and a city or region in ancient Mesopotamia. The Assyrians were the descendants of Assur, and he himself was a son of Shem. The region was named after the Assyrians, who were an important people in this area during biblical times.

in_english.name: Ashur
in_english.long_meaning: The name Ashur originates from the Hebrew Bible, referring to the eldest son of Shem, who was a son of Arphaxad and a grandson of Noah. Ashur is also the name of an ancient city or region in Mesopotamia, which was the center of the Assyrian Empire. The Assyrians were a Semitic people who established a powerful and influential empire in ancient times. The name Ashur symbolizes strength, resilience, and a connection to the rich history of the ancient Near East.

data.cultural_impact: The name Ashur carries a rich cultural history as it was the name of a major ancient civilization, the Assyrians, and the name of their chief god. Ashur was a powerful and significant deity in the ancient Middle Eastern pantheon. The Assyrian empire was known for its military prowess and advanced civilization, leaving a lasting impact on world history. The name Ashur remains a reminder of the ancient Assyrian civilization and its achievements.
data.spiritual_significance: For Christians, the spiritual significance of the name Ashur lies in its references in the Bible. Ashur is mentioned as the name of a place (2 Kings 13:4) and as the name of an Assyrian king (2 Kings 17:24). In these biblical references, Ashur represents the destination of Israelites who were taken captive and forced to live in exile. The name Ashur serves as a reminder of God's faithfulness and provision even in the midst of exile and hardship. It can also be seen as a call to trust in God's sovereignty and protection during difficult times.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Ashur in the Old Testament is associated with the ancient city of Ashur, the capital of the Assyrian Empire. Spiritually, it represents the human tendency to seek control and power over others, reflecting the Assyrian Empire's militaristic and expansionist nature. In Christianity, Ashur can symbolize the temptation to seek worldly dominion and the challenge to trust in God's providence instead.
